newsitem.title: UK: UK financial jobs rise 1st time since Sep 95 - CBI.
newsitem.headline: UK financial jobs rise 1st time since Sep 95 - CBI.

text.p: Employment in the UK's financial services sector rose in the three months to March, the first increase since September 1995, a survey by the Confederation of British Industry and Coopers and Lybrand said on Monday.

"The positive employment position reflects continuing strength in the capital markets sector and expansion of distribution capability in retail financial services, in response to more buoyant demand," said Pat Newberry, Coopers and Lybrand consulting practice partner.

Thirty-eight percent of firms said they had increased the numbers employed whilst 27 had reduced them, leaving a positive balance of 11 percent. This compared with negative balances of 9.0 percent in December and 29 in March 1996.
Business optimism recorded its fifth successive increase but the rise was the slowest since December 1995.
"This is an encouraging survey with rising employment and relatively buoyant business optimism and volumes," said CBI chief economic adviser Kate Barker.
"However, the survey does indicate a reduced tempo of growth, with a slight rise in the level of demand as a constraint on business over the coming year," she said.
Securities traders and life insurers noted the largest increases in business optimism with only general insurers noting a fall in confidence.

The survey showed a further rise in profitability but at a slower rate than in December when it increased by the quickest rate since September 1994. Higher profitability is now expected over the coming three months.

The volume of business rose moderately over the past three months, although not as quickly as the fourth quarter of last year, when it increased at the strongest rate since December 1989. Volumes rose most strongly with private individuals and financial institutions.
Newberry said that a further wave of mergers was likely in the retail sector because of over-capacity and a growing tendency for customers to show around.

Despite the apparent improvement in the employment position, cost pressures will remain intense as firms increase spending on advertising and continue to invest in information technology to develop efficient delivery and customer inflation systems, Newberry added.
The survey showed capital spending on land and buildings was expected to fall over the coming year, although IT investment intentions remained strong.
The most likely constraint on planned investment over the coming year is no an inadequate return on proposed investment which has fallen to its lowest level since June 1995.
The survey covered 302 financial services firms and was carried out between February 21 and March 12.
